examples.ko: 오래된 사진이 빛바래서 얼굴이 잘 안 보여요.
examples.en: The old photo has faded, so I can't see the faces well.

examples.ko: 할머니 방에는 빛바랜 가족사진이 걸려 있어요.
examples.en: A faded family photo hangs in my grandmother's room.
The curtains have faded in the sunlight.

examples.ko: 빛바랜 청바지를 일부러 사는 사람도 있어요.
examples.en: Some people buy faded jeans on purpose.
Even if the book cover fades, the contents stay the same.
This letter has faded, but it is precious to me.

explain: 오래돼서 색이 옅어진 사진, 종이, 옷에 써요. '빛바랜 사진'처럼 '-ㄴ' 형태로 가장 자주 들어요. 추억이나 명성이 희미해졌다는 비유로도 쓰는데, 이때는 글에서 더 많이 나와요.
explain_en: It is used for photos, paper and clothes whose color has become pale with age. You will most often hear the '-ㄴ' form, as in '빛바랜 사진'. It can also be used figuratively for memories or fame that have faded, mostly in writing.

examples.en: Rays of light come in through the gap in the window.

examples.ko: 아침 빛살에 눈이 부셔서 잠이 깼어요.
examples.en: The morning light was so bright in my eyes that I woke up.
Rays of light poured down between the leaves.
I rested for a moment in the warm rays of light.
When the clouds cleared, bright rays of light shone down.

examples.ko: 빛살 하나가 책상 위를 비추고 있어요.
examples.en: A single ray of light is shining on the desk.

explain: '햇빛'은 해에서 오는 빛 전체를 말하고, '빛살'은 가늘게 뻗은 줄기 같은 빛을 가리켜요. 해가 만든 빛살은 '햇살'이라고도 하는데, 일상 대화에서는 '햇살'이 더 자연스러워요.
explain_en: '햇빛' refers to light from the sun as a whole, while '빛살' points to light stretching out in thin beams. Beams made by the sun are also called '햇살', which sounds more natural in daily conversation.

examples.en: My younger sibling runs around outside all day.
Where do you keep running around every weekend?
The child scampers around the house.
I ran around all day, so I'm tired.

examples.ko: 그렇게 빨빨거리지 말고 좀 앉아 있어요.
examples.en: Stop running around like that and sit down for a bit.
The child who was scampering about suddenly got quiet.

explain: 가만히 있지 않고 부지런히 여기저기 돌아다니는 모습에 써요. 말투가 편하고 구어적이라서 격식을 차린 글에는 잘 안 맞아요. 활발한 아이나 바쁘게 다니는 사람을 말할 때 자주 어울려요.
explain_en: It describes someone who can't sit still and keeps going busily from place to place. The tone is casual and spoken, so it doesn't fit formal writing. It suits lively kids or people who are always on the move.

examples.en: Trees suck water up through their roots.
The child sucked the juice up through a straw.

examples.ko: 큰 펌프가 깊은 곳의 지하수를 빨아올리고 있어요.
examples.en: A big pump is drawing up groundwater from deep down.

examples.ko: 식물이 물을 빨아올리는 모습을 실험으로 봤어요.
examples.en: I saw a plant drawing up water in an experiment.
The sponge soaked up the water, so the floor dried.
You have to suck hard through the straw for the drink to come up.

explain: '빨아들이다'는 안쪽으로 끌어들이는 느낌이고, '빨아올리다'는 아래에 있는 것을 위로 끌어 올리는 느낌이 강해요. 뿌리, 빨대, 펌프처럼 물이 위로 올라가는 장면에 잘 어울려요.
explain_en: '빨아들이다' feels like pulling something inward, while '빨아올리다' stresses drawing something up from below. It fits scenes where liquid rises, such as roots, straws and pumps.

examples.ko: 문어 다리에는 빨판이 많이 달려 있어요.
examples.en: An octopus's legs have many suckers on them.
Thanks to its suckers, an octopus sticks to rocks.
You attach this toy to a window with its suction cup.

examples.ko: 물고기 중에는 빨판이 있는 종류도 있어요.
examples.en: Some kinds of fish have suckers.

examples.ko: 빨판을 이용해서 벽을 올라가는 동물이 있어요.
examples.en: There are animals that climb walls using suckers.

examples.ko: 빨판에 먼지가 묻으면 잘 안 붙어요.
examples.en: If dust gets on the suction cup, it doesn't stick well.

explain: 문어나 오징어 다리에 있는 동그란 부분을 말해요. 유리창에 붙이는 장난감이나 고리의 흡착 부분도 '빨판'이라고 부르는 경우가 많아요. 동물 이야기나 과학 수업에서 자주 나와요.
explain_en: It refers to the round parts on the legs of an octopus or squid. People also often call the suction part of window-mounted toys or hooks a '빨판'. It comes up a lot in animal talk and science classes.

examples.en: I starched the shirt and ironed it stiff.
I was so startled that my body went stiff.

examples.ko: 새 와이셔츠 깃이 빳빳이 서 있어요.
examples.en: The collar of the new dress shirt stands stiff.
He walked off with his head held stiffly high.

examples.ko: 햇볕에 널어 둔 수건이 빳빳이 말랐어요.
examples.en: The towel I hung in the sun dried stiff.
Please sit on the chair with your back held straight.

explain: '빳빳하다'에서 온 부사로, 구부러지지 않고 곧고 뻣뻣한 모습을 말해요. '빳빳하게'라고도 많이 말해요. '고개를 빳빳이 들다'는 겸손하지 않고 당당하거나 거만한 태도를 나타낼 때도 있어요.
explain_en: It is the adverb form of '빳빳하다' and describes something staying straight and stiff without bending. People also often say '빳빳하게'. '고개를 빳빳이 들다' can also show a proud or arrogant attitude.

examples.en: We grind red peppers to make chili powder.
My mother had rice ground at the mill and brought it back.
I use a mortar when I crush garlic.
Please grind the sesame seeds finely.
This machine grinds grain quickly.
I sprinkled the ground salt on the food.

explain: 곡식, 고추, 깨처럼 딱딱하거나 마른 것을 부수어 가루로 만들 때 써요. 절구로 콩이나 마늘을 두드려 부수는 건 '찧다'라고도 해요. 받침 'ㅎ' 때문에 '빻아요[빠아요]', '빻고[빠코]'처럼 발음이 달라지니 주의하세요.
explain_en: Use it when you break hard or dry things like grain, chili peppers or sesame seeds into powder. Pounding things such as garlic in a mortar can also be called '찧다'. Because of the final 'ㅎ', the pronunciation shifts in forms like '빻고[빠코]', so be careful.

examples.en: Sticky notes are packed tightly all over the wall.
The calendar is filled with appointments.
Students are sitting packed together in the classroom.
I wrote the letters closely packed in my notebook.
Books are crammed tightly on the shelf.

examples.ko: 주말 일정이 빼곡히 차 있어서 쉴 틈이 없어요.
examples.en: My weekend schedule is packed solid, so I have no time to rest.

explain: 빈틈없이 가득 찬 모습을 말하고, '빽빽이'와 비슷하게 써요. 글자, 책, 사람뿐 아니라 일정이 꽉 찬 것에도 자연스럽게 써요. 반대로 사이가 듬성듬성한 모습은 '듬성듬성'이라고 해요.
explain_en: It describes things filled with no gaps, and it is used much like '빽빽이'. It works naturally for letters, books and people, and also for a fully booked schedule. The opposite, sparsely spaced, is '듬성듬성'.

examples.en: That player's skill is outstanding.
The mountain scenery is really remarkable.
She is famous for her outstanding beauty.

examples.ko: 이 작가는 문장이 빼어나서 인기가 많아요.
examples.en: This writer's prose is superb, so he is very popular.
This is an exceptionally beautiful beach.
It's fine even if your grades aren't that outstanding.

explain: '뛰어나다'와 비슷하지만 경치, 미모, 솜씨처럼 아름답고 특별히 훌륭한 것에 더 어울려요. 글이나 방송 같은 조금 격식 있는 말투에서 많이 나와요. 일상 대화에서는 '뛰어나다'나 '멋지다'도 많이 써요.
explain_en: It is similar to '뛰어나다' but fits things that are both beautiful and exceptionally fine, such as scenery, looks and craftsmanship. It appears often in writing and broadcasts with a somewhat formal tone. In everyday talk, people also use '뛰어나다' or '멋지다'.

examples.en: The baby is hungry and keeps shrieking and crying.
Why are you talking in such a shrill voice?
My younger sibling squealed for the toy.
The baby who had been screeching all night finally fell asleep.
Stop shrieking and try speaking slowly.
The baby was screeching, so I couldn't finish the call.

explain: 그냥 '울다'보다 소리가 높고 날카로워서 듣는 사람이 시끄럽다고 느낄 때 써요. 주로 아기나 아이에게 쓰고, 어른에게 쓰면 무례하게 들려요. 소리 내는 모습이 계속될 때 '-거리다' 형태로 자주 써요.
explain_en: Compared with plain '울다' (to cry), the sound is higher and sharper, and the listener finds it noisy. It is mostly used for babies or children; about an adult it sounds rude. The '-거리다' form suggests the noise keeps going.

examples.ko: 책꽂이에는 교과서 외에도 소설책과 시집이 빽빽이 꽂혀 있어요.
examples.en: Besides textbooks, novels and poetry books are packed tightly on the bookshelf.

examples.ko: 버스 안에 사람들이 빽빽이 서 있어요.
examples.en: People are standing packed tightly inside the bus.
Trees stand densely packed in the forest.
I filled my notebook with tightly written notes.
Cars are parked bumper to bumper in the lot.

examples.ko: 좁은 사무실에 책상이 빽빽이 놓여 있어요.
examples.en: Desks are crammed tightly into the small office.

explain: 사이에 빈틈이 거의 없이 촘촘한 모습이에요. '빼곡히'와 아주 비슷하게 쓰고, 반대로 듬성듬성한 모습은 '듬성듬성'이라고 해요. 형용사 '빽빽하다'의 부사형이라서 '빽빽하게'라고도 말해요.
explain_en: It describes things placed very close together with almost no gaps. It is used much like '빼곡히', and the opposite is '듬성듬성' (sparsely). It is the adverb form of the adjective '빽빽하다', so '빽빽하게' also works.

examples.en: My younger sibling is showing off with a new bag on.

examples.ko: 시험 한 번 잘 봤다고 너무 뻐기지 마요.
examples.en: Don't brag so much just because you did well on one test.
He goes around bragging about how much money he has.
People who show off don't have many friends.
My older brother bragged about coming first, and it was annoying.
Please don't talk as if you're showing off.

explain: '자랑하다'는 좋은 뜻으로도 쓰지만, '뻐기다'는 잘난 척하며 거만하게 구는 느낌이 있어서 늘 부정적이에요. '뻐기+어'가 줄어서 '뻐겨요', '뻐겼어요'가 돼요. 보통 남이 그러는 걸 보고 얄밉다고 말할 때 써요.
explain_en: '자랑하다' can be positive, but '뻐기다' always sounds negative, as if someone acts arrogant and full of themselves. '뻐기+어' contracts to '뻐겨요' and '뻐겼어요'. You usually use it when you find someone else's showing off annoying.

examples.en: I can hear a cuckoo in the forest.

examples.ko: 뻐꾸기는 다른 새의 둥지에 알을 낳아요.
examples.en: Cuckoos lay their eggs in other birds' nests.
I woke up to the sound of a cuckoo calling in the morning.
The cuckoo clock in the living room chimes every hour.
I climbed the mountain and saw a cuckoo.
Is there another bird that calls like a cuckoo?

explain: 우는 소리가 '뻐꾹뻐꾹'처럼 들려요. '뻐꾸기시계'처럼 합성어로도 써요. 다른 새의 둥지에 알을 맡기는 습성이 있는 새예요.
explain_en: Its call sounds like '뻐꾹뻐꾹'. It also appears in compounds like '뻐꾸기시계' (cuckoo clock). It is a bird known for leaving its eggs in other birds' nests.

en: gape; open and close the mouth repeatedly (like a fish)

examples.en: The goldfish in the tank open and close their mouths.
The fish are gulping at the surface of the water.

examples.ko: 아이가 입을 뻐끔거리며 물고기 흉내를 냈어요.
examples.en: The child opened and closed their mouth, imitating a fish.
The carp gaped its mouth, begging for food.

examples.ko: 물 밖으로 나온 물고기가 계속 뻐끔거려요.
examples.en: The fish that came out of the water keeps gasping.

examples.ko: 입만 뻐끔거릴 뿐 말이 안 나왔어요.
examples.en: I only opened and closed my mouth, and no words came out.

explain: 물고기가 물속에서 입을 열었다 닫았다 하는 모습이 기본이에요. 사람에게 쓰면 소리는 안 나고 입 모양만 움직이는 모습이라서, 말소리가 들리는 '중얼거리다'와 달라요. 놀라거나 당황해서 말이 안 나올 때 비유로도 써요. '뻐끔대다'도 같은 말이에요.
explain_en: Its core image is a fish opening and closing its mouth in the water. For people it means the mouth moves with no sound coming out, unlike '중얼거리다' (to mumble), where you can hear words. It is also used figuratively when someone is too shocked or flustered to speak. '뻐끔대다' is the same word.

examples.en: My younger sibling has buck teeth and is getting braces.
Her buck teeth show a little when she smiles.
I worried about my buck teeth when I was little.
I had my buck teeth fixed at a dentist's office in a big hospital.
They say that actor's buck teeth are his charm.
The child with buck teeth smiled broadly.

explain: 앞니가 바깥쪽으로 튀어나온 이를 말해요. 놀리는 말처럼 들릴 수 있어서 상대방 앞에서는 조심해서 써야 해요. '덧니'는 이가 겹쳐서 하나 더 난 것이라서 서로 다른 말이에요.
explain_en: It refers to front teeth that stick out. It can sound like teasing, so be careful using it in front of someone. '덧니' is different: it means an extra tooth growing out of line.

examples.ko: 인공 눈물을 넣었더니 눈이 덜 뻑뻑해요.
examples.en: After I put in artificial tears, my eyes feel less dry and stiff.
The door is stiff, so it doesn't open easily.

examples.ko: 밥이 너무 뻑뻑해서 물을 더 넣었어요.
examples.en: The rice was too thick and dry, so I added more water.

examples.ko: 자전거 체인이 뻑뻑하면 기름을 쳐야 해요.
examples.en: If the bicycle chain is stiff, you need to oil it.
If the dough is too thick, add a little water.
The drawer was sticking. Could you take a look at it?

explain: 물기나 기름기가 적어서 잘 움직이지 않거나 잘 풀어지지 않는 느낌이에요. 문, 서랍, 반죽, 눈 모두에 써요. 반대 느낌은 '부드럽다'로 말하면 돼요.
explain_en: It describes something that doesn't move or loosen easily because it lacks moisture or oil. It works for doors, drawers, dough and eyes alike. For the opposite feeling, you can say '부드럽다'.

examples.ko: 그 집은 겉만 뻔지르르하지 속은 비었어요.
examples.en: That house looks slick only on the outside, and it's empty inside.
He's all slick talk and no action.
Don't be fooled by flashy packaging.
That shop has a flashy sign and nothing more.
He came out dressed up in flashy clothes.
It looks glossy, but the quality isn't great.

explain: 겉모양은 매끄럽고 번듯한데 속은 별로일 때 부정적으로 써요. '말만 뻔지르르하다', '겉만 뻔지르르하다'처럼 겉과 속이 다르다는 말과 자주 같이 나와요. '번지르르하다'로도 말해요.
explain_en: It is used negatively when something looks smooth and impressive on the outside but is poor inside. It often appears in phrases like '말만 뻔지르르하다' and '겉만 뻔지르르하다', stressing that the outside and inside differ. People also say '번지르르하다'.
